catalog_quote: 5.3.1. High pitch, length and stress are non-phonemic. They are closely linked in that stress always occurs with length, and usually with high pitch. High pitch and length can occur without stress. High pitch occurs on the anti-penultimate and/or on the penultimate syllables of words. High pitch and stress are influenced by intonational patterns. 5.3.2. Stress is predictable. (1) It occurs on the penultimate syllable of 2 - 11 syllable words. (2) An exception occurs with a low-high vowel sequence of two moras in antipenultimate and penultimate positions, when the stress always occurs on the first vowel. /ga.uda/ [gáudʌ] 'poison stone' /ba.i/ [bái] 'crossbeam' /kua.iba/ [kʷáibʌ] 'bark' (3) Secondary stress occurs on the first syllable of the stem in 4 - 11 syllable words. /galuʔeta/ [gàluʔétʌ] 'dog'

High pitch and stress are influenced by intonational patterns.' 5.3.2 'Stress is predictable…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and predictable: primary stress (accompanied by length and usually high pitch) falls on the penultimate syllable of any polysyllabic word; when the antepenult and penult vowels form a low-to-high (rising-sonority a+i, a+u type) two-mora vowel sequence, stress falls on the first vowel of that sequence (i.e. surfaces on the antepenultimate vowel, e.g. [gáuda]).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on the first syllable of the stem in words of 4-11 syllables (e.g. [gàluʔéta] 'dog').
new_statements.exceptions: Low-high bimoraic vowel sequence spanning antepenult+penult: stress on its first vowel ([gáuda] 'poison stone', [bái] 'crossbeam', [kʷáiba] 'bark'). High pitch may sit on antepenult and/or penult and, with stress, is affected by intonation (interrogative pattern 'accentuates' stress, p.25-26). Sec. 4.2.1 (p.6-7) notes CuV must be monosyllabic or stress would appear antepenultimate ([gikʷékʷa] 'he gathers').
new_statements.domain_note: Stated for words of 2-11 syllables (phonemic word, citation transcriptions); Huckett 1974:85,87-88 adds that a verb phrase (verb + adverb + object suffix; idiomatic Sub+V) forms a single stress group with stress on the penultimate syllable of the group, so the stress domain can extend over the close-knit verb phrase.
new_statements.identity_note: Sampson & Huckett 1965 describe the Central dialect of 'Vivigana' (= Iduna, idun1242, iso viv), data from Wakonai village near Vivigani airstrip, eastern Goodenough Island; they note nine dialects and compared five others plus closely related Bwaidoga (bwai1242). Huckett 1974 likewise: 'Iduna (Vivigani) language (Central dialect)'. Language-level match to idun1242.

sources.note: Sec. 5.3 Suprasegmental items, p.25: high pitch, length and stress are non-phonemic; stress is predictable, on the penultimate syllable of 2-11 syllable words; exception: a low-high two-mora vowel sequence in antepenult+penult takes stress on its first vowel ([gáuda], [bái], [kwáiba]); secondary stress on the first syllable of the stem in 4-11 syllable words ([gàlu?éta] 'dog'). Sec. 4.2.1 p.6-7 uses the penultimate-stress rule to argue CuV (labialised C) is one syllable. p.20-21: /a/ = [a] stressed, [ʌ] unstressed; p.29: possible vowel length only in first syllable of trisyllables (unsolved).
